learningObjective: Explain why DistMult must assign the same score to an antisymmetric relation and its reversed triple, while the complex conjugate in ComplEx removes that forced equality.
mediumRationale: A deterministic two-panel SVG is the smallest medium that can keep one directed fact fixed while aligning the two models' swapped score expressions. The side-by-side arrows and algebra expose an impossibility caused by the operator, not embedding width, without adding controls or repeating the article's broader capability table.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected: a graph can show the true and reversed edges, but Mermaid cannot align the exact score expressions closely enough to prove why one swap is invariant and the other is not.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected: deterministic coordinates align identical entity swaps, direct edge labels, and the two score pairs so the algebraic constraint is visible and checkable.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: a table could compare the equations accessibly, but it would not keep the true directed fact and false reversed fact spatially stable across both operators; the article already contains the appropriate broad comparison table.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: changing entities, dimensions, or relation types would add state without changing the universal commutativity argument and would weaken print completeness.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: the local deck and reviewed papers contain related tensor, model, and relation-pattern figures, but no external figure is needed. Figure reuse permission was not relied upon; the entities, edge example, layout, wording, and paired derivation are original.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: the prose states that DistMult is symmetric and ComplEx is not, but readers still have to mentally perform the entity swap and see why additional dimensions cannot change the equality.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is that representational limits follow from score algebra rather than model width. For DistMult, sum_i h_i r_i t_i equals sum_i t_i r_i h_i because multiplication of real scalars commutes in every dimension, so a true antisymmetric fact and its reversal must tie. ComplEx instead scores Re(sum_i h_i r_i conjugate(t_i)); swapping head and tail moves the conjugate, so equality is no longer an identity and the true direction may outrank its reversal. The original Ada-parent_of-Ben example isolates this one invariant; the existing article table retains the broader four-model comparison.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages and visually inspected pages 117-119, then checked the primary TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, and RotatE sources before selecting an original score-swap proof.

implementation.accessibility: Each panel has a linked heading plus an SVG title and detailed description that state the true edge, false reversed edge, equations, and inference. Solid versus dashed arrows, arrow direction, direct true/false labels, written equations, and explicit outcomes preserve the lesson without color. The established two-panel primitive stacks below 640 pixels; each SVG uses a compact 300-unit viewBox with no minimum width or horizontal scroll, and its smallest edge labels are explicitly raised to 11 SVG units for readability at 390 CSS pixels. Existing theme variables preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print tokens force a light high-contrast palette and keep the figure together.
